hook.text: Most adult humans can't digest milk. Drinking it is a genetic mutation that spread in dairying cultures.

buildup.text: All baby mammals digest milk using lactase enzyme. In most species, that enzyme shuts off after weaning.

discovery.text: About 8,000 years ago, a mutation let some Europeans keep producing lactase into adulthood.

twist.text: This happened independently in East Africa too—different mutation, same result. Milk was that valuable.

climax.text: Lactose tolerance spread rapidly because milk drinkers survived famines better—a huge survival advantage.

punchline.text: Most humans are lactose intolerant. Milk drinkers are the mutants.

quiz.question: Why did lactose tolerance spread in dairying populations?
options: Milk drinkers survived famines better, giving them a survival advantage

details.summary: The dairy revolution traces how humans evolved lactose tolerance and built a massive global industry around milk, cheese, butter, and yogurt. This topic covers the genetics of lactose persistence, dairy farming's expansion, and its central role in modern nutrition.
details.whyItMatters: Dairy provides critical nutrition for over 6 billion people and supports 150 million farming households. The genetic mutation enabling adult milk digestion gave some populations a significant survival advantage.
takeaways: Lactose tolerance evolved independently in European, African, and Middle Eastern populations
Only about 35% of the world's adult population can fully digest lactose
Global dairy production exceeds 900 million tonnes of milk annually

faq.question: Why can some adults digest milk while others cannot?
faq.answer: A genetic mutation called lactase persistence allows some adults to continue producing the enzyme that breaks down milk sugar. This evolved independently in populations that relied heavily on dairy, giving them a nutritional advantage.

faq.question: How did dairy farming become a global industry?
faq.answer: Advances in refrigeration, pasteurization, and transportation in the 19th and 20th centuries transformed dairy from a local farmstead activity into a global industry with standardized products, factory-scale processing, and international trade.
